page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: A substance added to an emulsion to make
it stable is called an emulsifying agent
Without it the two liquids separate into
steps.why: An emulsion of two liquids that do not mix is not stable by itself: the small droplets join into larger ones and the two liquids form separate layers. The emulsifying agent is the third substance added to stop that, so stability is the whole point of the definition.
common_mistakes: Writing that the emulsifying agent makes the two liquids mix. They still do not mix; the agent only keeps the droplets separate.

Calling it a catalyst. The emulsifying agent stays in the emulsion as part of it, held at the surface between the two liquids; a catalyst takes part in a reaction and is recovered unchanged at the end.
steps.memory_tip: Emulsifier equals stabiliser. Its one job is to stop the droplets joining.
steps.margin_note: The word stabilise carries this mark. A definition without it reads as a description of any additive.

steps.label: How it acts, with examples

lines.text: Ex: soap in a kerosene and water emulsion.

lines: The agent collects at the surface between
the two liquids and lowers the interfacial
tension, so the droplets stay separate.
For oil in water: soaps, detergents,
For water in oil: heavy metal salts of
fatty acids and long chain alcohols.
steps.why: The agent has one part with affinity for water and one part with affinity for oil, so it settles at the surface between the two liquids and stays there. A film of it around each droplet lowers the interfacial tension and keeps the droplets from joining, which is why the same soap that forms micelles also acts as an emulsifier.
common_mistakes: Giving a water in oil agent for an oil in water emulsion. Soaps and detergents belong to the oil in water type.
Writing that the agent dissolves the oil. It surrounds the oil droplets; it does not dissolve them.
steps.memory_tip: One part of the agent has affinity for water, the other for oil, so it sits at the surface between them.
steps.margin_note: One named example is enough. Adding the interfacial tension line is what makes it a two-mark answer.

insider_note: Most answers stop at "a substance added to stabilise an emulsion". The second mark is for saying where the agent goes, at the surface between the two liquids, and naming one example.
